questions.title: How can fair use be decided on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without discovery?
questions.question_body: The panel affirms dismissal at the pleading stage on fair use, citing TCA Television and Cariou. I'm confused about what materials a court can consider at 12(b)(6) to resolve fair use as a matter of law. Here, the court relied on the complaint, exhibits, incorporated videos, and judicially noticed copyright registrations. What are the limits on considering the actual videos (original Cameos and JKL segments) at this stage? Is there a risk the court is resolving disputed facts about purpose/market harm that normally would require evidence?

questions.title: Does the fact that Kimmel instigated the Cameo scripts defeat transformativeness?
questions.question_body: Santos argued Kimmel "instigated the creation" by submitting prompts under aliases, implying the secondary user designed the original purpose. The court rejects this, focusing on what a reasonable observer would perceive in the secondary use, and not on subjective intent (citing Warhol). Do courts ever consider who engineered the underlying content in assessing whether the later use is transformative, especially when the 'original' was created at the secondary user's direction? How does that square with cases like Campbell (parody) where the original wasn’t authored at the parodist’s behest?

questions.title: What role does bad faith or deception play in fair use after Harper & Row?
questions.question_body: Santos claimed Kimmel’s false identities on Cameo showed bad faith that should vitiate fair use, citing Harper & Row’s "good faith" language. The court says the Supreme Court has distanced itself from that doctrine and focuses instead on non-supplanting commentary. What is the current Second Circuit (and Supreme Court) doctrine on bad faith in fair use? Can deception ever tip factor one or four against fair use, and under what circumstances would misrepresentation matter?

questions.title: Why doesn’t airing the Cameos on national TV cause cognizable market harm under factor four?
questions.question_body: The court says the relevant question is whether JKL usurped the market by offering a competing substitute, not whether criticism devalues Santos’s videos. But if Santos sells these exact videos on Cameo, didn’t JKL’s broadcast supply them to a broader audience for free, potentially undermining demand? How does the analysis differentiate between substitutive use of the same content and non-substitutive commentary, and what evidentiary showing is required at the pleading stage to allege market usurpation?

questions.title: What did the court mean by treating the Cameos as 'published' for factor two?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes the copyright registrations show the videos were published the same day they were created and cites 17 U.S.C. § 101. How does the court infer 'publication' from the registrations, and why does that matter to the nature-of-the-work factor? Are Cameo deliveries to a single purchaser 'publication,' or is there a separate distribution/broadcast requirement? How significant is the published/unpublished distinction after Harper & Row in modern digital contexts?

questions.title: Why did Santos lack standing to sue on the Cameo Terms of Service under Illinois law?
questions.question_body: The direct breach claim fails because Santos isn’t a party to the user Terms of Service (which govern Kimmel’s account) and Illinois law has a strong presumption against third-party beneficiaries absent an 'almost express' declaration. What specific language in typical platform TOS would be sufficient to make a non-party creator like Santos an intended third-party beneficiary? Does the presence of third-party-beneficiary language elsewhere in the TOS weigh against implying beneficiary status for other provisions as a matter of Illinois contract interpretation?

questions.title: What was missing from the New York implied-in-fact contract claim tied to the TOS?
questions.question_body: The court says Santos failed to plead the essential terms and a meeting of the minds that Kimmel would adhere to the TOS vis-à-vis Santos. If Santos had alleged that he accepted Kimmel’s orders only on the condition that purchasers comply with Cameo’s usage restrictions, would that suffice to plead an implied-in-fact agreement under New York law? What kinds of conduct or communications (course of dealing, notices on profile pages, order confirmations) have courts treated as manifesting mutual assent in analogous platform contexts?

questions.title: Why did the fraudulent inducement claim fail for lack of out-of-pocket loss under New York law?
questions.question_body: The panel affirms dismissal because Santos didn’t allege any out-of-pocket pecuniary loss, citing Lama Holding and Connaughton. If Santos spent time creating the videos and received payment, could he allege a net loss (e.g., time/value of services exceeding the price, or lost opportunities) that qualifies as out-of-pocket damages? Are reputational harms or diminution of the videos’ value cognizable in fraud, or are those barred as benefit-of-the-bargain or consequential damages in New York?
